keyTakeaways: Raksha Bandhan means "the tie of protection": the sister asks for her brother's long life on his right wrist, and he takes on a standing duty toward her.
In McKim Marriott's 1950-52 ethnography of Kishan Garhi, the thread was still tied by Brahman priests onto paying patrons; only "a few sisters" had begun tying it on brothers.
The sisters' own half of that festival, Saluno, used young barley shoots rather than thread, and brothers reciprocated with small coins.
The Rani Karnavati and Humayun story has no settled historical basis: a professor of religious studies calls its veracity "a matter of debate among scholars".

The mailable rakhi is 75 years old, not new, and the private version of the same instinct is still measurable: 44.2% of SubhSandesh creators password-protect a page before sharing it (1,315 of 2,973).

faqs.question: Why is Raksha Bandhan always on the full moon of Shravan?
faqs.answer: Because the text that first prescribes the rite fixes it there. Chapter 137 of the Uttara Parva of the Bhavishya Purana has Krishna specify the purnima of Shravana, at sunrise, for the binding of a raksha. In village practice the same full moon also closed the fortnight when married daughters visited their parents, so the calendar and the family visit lined up.

faqs.question: Is there a correct time of day to tie the rakhi?
faqs.answer: The Bhavishya Purana account has the bath at sunrise and the protective packet prepared in the early afternoon, between roughly noon and 3 pm. Precision has always mattered to people who could get it: McKim Marriott records brothers in electrified Namhalli, near Bangalore, tuning in to All India Radio for a time signal so they could tie the charm at the astrologically exact moment.

faqs.question: Why is it called a tie of protection when the sister is the one tying it?
faqs.answer: Because the thread is the request, not the protection. Her spoken line is a wish for his long life; what she gets in exchange is his standing obligation afterwards. Vinay Lal of UCLA reads the whole rite as a woman reasserting her ties to her natal home, and signalling to her husband's family that she has people.

faqs.question: Can a woman tie a rakhi to someone who is not her brother?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is normal rather than a modern relaxation. Lal records the muh boli behen, a sister in every respect except biology, cousins standing in where there are no sisters, and rakhis tied on prime ministers and soldiers. Times of India advertisements in Mumbai on 25 August 1999 urged readers to send threads to troops in Kargil.

faqs.question: What can a woman do on Raksha Bandhan if she has no brother?
faqs.answer: The customary answer is to make a brother, not to skip the day. A cousin, a close friend or a colleague can be tied a rakhi, and the obligation is treated as real once accepted. Sisters also tie each other, and SubhSandesh has a separate post on celebrating Raksha Bandhan without a brother.

faqs.question: Can a sister tie a rakhi to another sister?
faqs.answer: Nothing in the rite requires a man on the receiving end, and sister-to-sister rakhi is now widely practised. The scriptural version has a priest tying it to a patron and the village version has sisters honouring brothers, so neither is a rule about gender so much as a record of who held the power to help. Treat it as a live custom rather than a scriptural prescription.

faqs.question: Why is the return gift an odd amount like 101 or 501 rupees?
faqs.answer: The extra rupee is the auspicious part. Lal records the customary sums as 51, 101, 251 or 501 rupees. The gift is not payment for the thread; it closes the asymmetry, on the same logic as the small coins Marriott's Saluno brothers handed over in exchange for barley shoots.

faqs.question: Does a store-bought rakhi count, or should it be handmade?
faqs.answer: Store-bought has been part of the ritual for at least seventy-five years. Marriott recorded factory-made charms of priestly type being hawked around Kishan Garhi by a local caste group of Jogis in 1950-52, and it was those bought threads that sisters began tying on their brothers. The provenance of the string was never the point.

faqs.question: Is sending a rakhi by post or as a link a modern shortcut?
faqs.answer: No, and the field record is unusually clear on this. Marriott wrote in 1955 that the new string charms were "more convenient for mailing in letters to distant, city-dwelling brothers whom sisters cannot visit on the auspicious day". Posting the rakhi is roughly as old as sisters tying it themselves.

faqs.question: How long should a rakhi stay on the wrist?
faqs.answer: None of the sources used here prescribes a removal date, so the common rules of thumb are custom rather than text. Families vary between a few days, until it falls off, and keeping it until the next festival. If someone in your family has a rule, that rule is the answer.

faqs.question: Is Raksha Bandhan only for Hindus?
faqs.answer: In practice, no. Rabindranath Tagore had Hindus and Muslims tie rakhis on each other on 16 October 1905 against the partition of Bengal, including maulvis in a Kolkata mosque. Mathew Schmalz, an American Catholic and a professor of religious studies, has been tied a rakhi by two sisters of a Varanasi household for thirty years.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Why Does a Sister Tie Rakhi on Her Brother? The Real Origin

A sister ties a rakhi on her brother's right wrist to put him under a protective vow and to renew her claim on the family she was born into. She asks for his long life; he takes on a standing duty to stand behind her. That is the answer — but it is not the original rite. When McKim Marriott recorded the festival in the Uttar Pradesh village of Kishan Garhi in 1950–52, the thread was still tied by Brahman priests onto patrons' wrists for cash, and only "a few sisters" had begun tying priest-style charms onto brothers, partly because a factory string could be posted to a brother in the city. That private, addressed impulse is still measurable: 44.2% of SubhSandesh creators password-protect a page before sharing it (1,315 of 2,973), and 51.1% of 36,202 recorded views land on a phone. Five layers, separated below.

## What "Raksha Bandhan" means, and why the right wrist

*Raksha* is protection and *bandhan* is a bond, so the festival's name translates as "the tie of protection". The thread is an obligation, not an ornament. It goes on the right wrist because in Hindu ritual the right hand is the hand of action and of giving — the hand that takes the tilak and extends to accept a vow.

The sequence matters as much as the thread itself. Vinay Lal, professor of history at UCLA, [records the standard order](https://southasia.ucla.edu/culture/festivals/raksha-bandhan/): a tilak on the brother's forehead, aarti with a lamp turned clockwise, then the thread, then a sweet placed in his mouth. The Punjabi line that accompanies it runs *"Behen ne rakhi bandhi / Bhai tu chir jug jee"* — the sister tied the rakhi; brother, may you live long.

Notice the direction: her line is a wish for his lifespan. The protection she is buying sits not in the thread but in what he owes her afterwards.

## The five layers behind the ritual, separated

Most explanations stack stories from different centuries into one paragraph and label the result "ancient". They are five separate things, and they entered the rite at different times.

### 1. The scriptural layer — a priest tied it to a king

The oldest textual instruction has no sister in it. Chapter 137 of the Uttara Parva of the [Bhavishya Purana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhavishya_Purana) has Krishna describe a *raksha* bound to the right wrist on the Shravan full moon by the *rajapurohita*, the royal priest, with the words "I am binding raksha to you with the same true words with which I bound Mahabali, King of the Asuras."

Marriott found that text still governing practice in 1950–52. On Charm Tying day in Kishan Garhi the Brahman domestic priests went to each patron and tied on his wrist "a charm in the form of a polychrome thread", and were paid in cash, "for it is thought impious to accept anything as a free gift from a priest."

### 2. The village layer — barley shoots, not thread

The sister-brother rite that fell on the same day had a different, regional name: Saluno. It closed the annual fortnight during which married daughters returned to their parents' village. At its end, [Marriott's field record](https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.504848) states, "the wives as well as their unmarried village sisters express their concern for and devotion to their brothers by placing young shoots of barley, the locally sacred grain, on the heads and ears of their brothers," and the brothers "reciprocate with small coins" — because a brother should accept nothing from a sister as a free gift.

So the sisters' half of the festival was about grain and a visit home. Not a bracelet.

### 3. The legend layer — Draupadi, Karnavati, and what is attested

Two stories carry the popular explanation. In one, Draupadi binds a strip of cloth on Krishna's bleeding finger and he owes her protection ever after. In the other, Rani Karnavati of Chittor sends a rakhi to the Mughal emperor Humayun in 1535, making him her brother so he will defend her city.

Mathew Schmalz, professor of religious studies at the College of the Holy Cross, is [blunt about the second](https://theconversation.com/explaining-rakshabandhan-a-hindu-festival-that-celebrates-the-brother-sister-bond-81665): "the historical veracity of this story remains a matter of debate among scholars" — and Humayun's troops did not arrive in time to save Chittorgarh. It is a good story about a bond crossing religion, not evidence for where the ritual came from.

### 4. The political layer — 16 October 1905

Rakhi has been turned into a public instrument at least once. Rabindranath Tagore used it against Curzon's partition of Bengal: on 16 October 1905, the day the partition took effect, he declared national mourning, bathed in the Ganga, then [walked through Kolkata tying rakhis](https://scroll.in/magazine/846275/in-bengal-the-bond-of-rakhi-once-symbolised-eternal-protection-between-hindus-and-muslims) on everyone he met, including the maulvis inside a mosque south of his own house.

That day inverted the rite: no sisters, no brothers, no family at all — the thread bound Hindus and Muslims to each other's safety.

### 5. The modern layer — the mailable thread, then the link

The form everyone now calls traditional appears in Marriott's notes as a novelty still spreading. Factory-made charms of priestly type were being hawked around Kishan Garhi by a local caste group of Jogis: "A few sisters in Kishan Garhi have taken to tying these heterogenetic charms of priestly type onto their brothers' wrists. The new string charms are also more convenient for mailing in letters to distant, city-dwelling brothers whom sisters cannot visit on the auspicious day."

A few sisters — partly because the object now fit inside an envelope. Marriott also notes brothers in electrified Namhalli, near Bangalore, tuning in to All India Radio for a time signal so they could tie their own charms at the astrologically exact moment. The medium has been reshaping this rite for seventy-five years, which is why a [Raksha Bandhan page addressed to one brother](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-rakshabandhan-to-brother) belongs in the same line as the posted string.

## How a rakhi reaches a brother who is not in the room

Four of those five layers answer one logistical question: the sister is somewhere else on the day. Here is what each solution delivers.

| How it reaches him | Earliest record of this form | Addressed to him alone? | Where it gets opened |
|---|---|---|---|
| She ties it herself | Saluno, Kishan Garhi, 1950–52 | Yes — she is in the room | On his wrist |
| A priest ties it, he pays | *Bhavishyottara Purana*; still standard in 1950–52 | No — every patron, one round | On his wrist |
| Factory string posted in a letter | Kishan Garhi, 1950–52 | Yes, if she writes the letter | Wherever the post finds him |
| Forwarded image on WhatsApp | Widespread by the 2010s | No — one file, many brothers | 51.1% of 36,202 views on a phone |
| A personalised page link | Current | 44.2% are password-protected (1,315 of 2,973) | 51.1% of 36,202 views on a phone |

Every form addressed to one brother required the sister to do specific work. The forwarded image is the only entry that removed the work and the address at once.

## Why the brother, and not a father or a husband

Because of where a married daughter's leverage sits. North Indian village exogamy sends a bride out of her natal village, and her parents customarily do not visit her married home. The brother stays, and is the standing intermediary. Lal reads rakhi precisely as "an occasion for reasserting a woman's ties to her natal home" — a signal to her husband's family that she has people.

How dependable is that signal? Shruti Chaudhry's ethnography in rural Uttar Pradesh, [published in *Modern Asian Studies* in 2019](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/for-how-long-can-your-ip%C4%ABharw%C4%81le-iintervene-accessing-natal-kin-s/), compares regional with cross-regional marriages and finds geographic distance "cuts women off from vital structures of support". Even for brides married nearby, support proved conditional on caste, class, poverty, the gender of her children, honour, and her stage in the life-course. Only the abstract is readable, so that is all this cites.

That is the honest version of the vow: a rakhi asserts a claim. It does not guarantee the claim will be honoured.

## What the brother owes back

Money, mostly, and specifically. Lal records the customary return gift as a small odd sum — ₹51, ₹101, ₹251 or ₹501 — the extra rupee being the auspicious part. It is not payment. It closes the asymmetry, on the same logic as the small coins Marriott's Saluno brothers handed over for barley shoots.

The obligation is not confined to blood. Lal notes the *muh boli behen*, a sister in every respect except biology, and rakhis tied on prime ministers and on soldiers: advertisements in the *Times of India* in Mumbai on 25 August 1999 urged readers to send threads to troops in Kargil and to the widows of the Kargil dead. Schmalz, an American Catholic, has been tied a rakhi by two sisters of a Varanasi household for thirty years.

## When the physical thread beats anything digital

If she can reach his wrist, she should. The rite is haptic — tilak, lamp, thread, sweet — and a link cannot put kumkum on a forehead. A brother in the same city who gets a URL instead will read it as a shortcut, and he will be right.

A posted rakhi also wins for a brother who does not use a smartphone, or is somewhere a page will not load. Our own 51.1% mobile figure also means nearly half of views are not on a phone, and a recipient with no device sits outside the number entirely. Sending both is the normal answer: the thread for the wrist, a page for the sentences she would never type into a WhatsApp group.

Where a page earns its place is the case Marriott described in 1952 — a brother in another city on the wrong day. Then the comparison is a forwarded image, not her hands, and picking from the [full set of greeting templates](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) costs about what writing the letter used to.

## Sources

- McKim Marriott, "Little Communities in an Indigenous Civilization", in *Village India: Studies in the Little Community* (Asia Publishing House, 1955), p. 204 — [full text, Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.504848)
- Mathew N. Schmalz, ["Explaining 'Rakshabandhan'"](https://theconversation.com/explaining-rakshabandhan-a-hindu-festival-that-celebrates-the-brother-sister-bond-81665), The Conversation, 4 August 2017 (updated 14 August 2019)
- Shruti Chaudhry, ["'For how long can your pīharwāle intervene?': Accessing natal kin support in rural North India"](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/for-how-long-can-your-ip%C4%ABharw%C4%81le-iintervene-accessing-natal-kin-s/), *Modern Asian Studies*, 2019 — abstract only
- Vinay Lal, ["Raksha Bandhan"](https://southasia.ucla.edu/culture/festivals/raksha-bandhan/), MANAS, UCLA (no date given)
- Deepanjan Ghosh, ["In Bengal, the bond of Rakhi once symbolised eternal protection"](https://scroll.in/magazine/846275/in-bengal-the-bond-of-rakhi-once-symbolised-eternal-protection-between-hindus-and-muslims), Scroll.in, 7 August 2017

failed.item: At least 3 first-party facts appear, and at least 2 are in the first 150 words
failed.why: Four first-party facts appear and two (44.2% password-protect, 51.1% mobile) sit inside the first 150 words, so the count is met — but every one of them is platform-wide, not rakhi-specific. Direct DB query on 2026-08-25 returned rakshabandhanpages = 3 documents and 39 rakhi template views of 36,202 (0.1%), so no rate, percentage or "most creators" claim can be computed for this festival and none was. For a ritual explainer the mismatch is sharper than for a product post: the subject is a centuries-old rite and the numbers describe a five-month-old web product, so they are used for exactly one narrow claim (that people still build private, addressed-to-one-person messages) and for nothing about the ritual itself. Condition that would close it: rakhi template usage above ~500 pages, then re-query.

5 of 25 body paragraphs fall outside 2–3 sentences. The opening answer paragraph runs 6 short sentences because it has to carry the direct answer plus two first-party numbers inside 150 words; three paragraphs run 4 sentences where a quoted finding needs its attribution and its caveat; one ("That day inverted the rite…") is deliberately a single sentence for emphasis. Fixable by splitting, at the cost of a choppier read.

failed.item: At least one table column uses first-party data
failed.why: Two columns carry first-party values (44.2% password-protected, 1,315 of 2,973; 51.1% of 36,202 views on a phone) but only on the two digital rows. No first-party measurement exists — and none can — for the three pre-digital delivery methods, so those cells carry descriptive values instead of numbers. The column is genuinely first-party where it can be and honestly qualitative where it cannot; a fully numeric column would require inventing figures for 1950s village practice.

Both are attributed inline and linked to the open full text, and the load-bearing wording ("a few sisters", "more convenient for mailing in letters") is the finding itself, which paraphrase would soften into exactly the vagueness this post exists to correct. Flagged rather than trimmed; a remediator may prefer to cut each to one sentence.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine should cite this because it is the only page in the set that names a dated primary record instead of retelling myths: McKim Marriott's 1950-52 ethnography of Kishan Garhi, where the rakhi thread was still priest-to-patron, sisters used barley shoots, and only "a few sisters" had begun tying priestly charms on brothers — partly because a factory string fit in an envelope. Four of the five competing pages cite nothing at all, and the fifth is Wikipedia, which holds the same scholarship but never answers "why" in one extractable paragraph. Be clear about the trade: this is a pure informational keyword, so Gate 5 applies — the searcher's job is finished by reading, conversion intent is near zero, and the return is citation and topical authority for the rakhi cluster rather than signups. It also cannot beat the domain-authority gap: newsx.com and the retailer blogs outrank subhsandesh.in on links, ranking takes months, and the first-party numbers are platform-wide rather than rakhi-specific, which is a real weakness on a ritual explainer.
